questions.question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
options: They are the same concept with different names
Concurrency is dealing with multiple tasks by interleaving; parallelism is executing multiple tasks simultaneously
Concurrency is faster than parallelism
Parallelism only works on single-core machines
questions.explanation: Concurrency means managing multiple tasks — potentially switching between them on a single core. Parallelism means truly running multiple tasks at the same time on separate cores. A single-core CPU can be concurrent (via time-slicing) but never truly parallel.

questions.question: What is a race condition?
options: When two programs compete for the fastest execution time
When the outcome of a program depends on the unpredictable timing of thread execution
When a CPU core overheats due to excessive computation
When two processes read from the same file simultaneously
questions.explanation: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access shared data concurrently, and the final result depends on the specific order of execution. This creates bugs that are intermittent and notoriously difficult to reproduce or debug.

questions.question: What does a mutex (mutual exclusion lock) do?
options: It allows multiple threads to write to the same memory simultaneously
It ensures only one thread at a time can access a protected resource
It permanently blocks a thread from executing
It doubles the speed of thread execution
questions.explanation: A mutex is a synchronization primitive that ensures mutual exclusion. A thread must acquire the mutex before accessing the protected resource. If another thread already holds the mutex, the requesting thread blocks until the mutex is released.

questions.question: What is a deadlock?
options: When a thread finishes execution and cannot be restarted
When two or more threads are each waiting for a resource held by another, creating a cycle where none can proceed
When a thread runs infinitely in a tight loop
When the CPU runs out of available cores
questions.explanation: Deadlock occurs when threads form a circular chain of resource dependencies. Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1. Neither can proceed, and the application hangs silently with no error or crash.

questions.question: In the Dining Philosophers problem, what strategy prevents deadlock?
options: Give each philosopher three forks instead of two
Impose an ordering rule: always pick up the lower-numbered fork first
Remove all forks from the table
Let each philosopher eat without needing any forks
questions.explanation: By imposing a global ordering on resource acquisition (always pick up the lower-numbered fork first), you break the circular wait condition. At least one philosopher will find their first fork already taken and will wait, preventing the deadlock cycle from forming.

questions.question: How does async/await differ from traditional multi-threading for handling I/O-bound work?
options: Async/await creates more threads than multi-threading
Async/await suspends the function at I/O points and frees the thread for other work, rather than blocking a dedicated thread per operation
Async/await eliminates the need for an operating system
Async/await is only used in JavaScript and cannot be used in other languages
questions.explanation: With async/await, when a function encounters an I/O operation (network call, disk read), it suspends execution and yields the thread back to the runtime. The thread can then execute other tasks. When the I/O completes, the function resumes. This avoids dedicating a blocked thread per pending I/O operation.

questions.question: What is a thread pool and why is it preferred over creating threads on-demand?
options: A thread pool is a collection of unused CPU cores
A thread pool pre-creates a fixed set of reusable worker threads, avoiding the overhead of constantly creating and destroying threads
A thread pool is a backup system that activates when the main thread crashes
A thread pool compresses multiple threads into a single thread
questions.explanation: Thread creation and destruction are expensive OS operations. A thread pool creates a fixed number of threads upfront. Incoming tasks are placed in a queue, and idle workers pick them up. This amortizes creation cost, bounds memory usage, and provides predictable concurrency limits.

questions.question: Two threads execute this code on a shared variable `count = 0`: Thread A runs `count = count + 1` and Thread B runs `count = count + 1`. Both operations involve read-then-write. What are the possible final values of count?
options: Always 2
Either 1 or 2, depending on interleaving
Always 1
Either 0, 1, or 2
questions.explanation: If both threads read count=0 before either writes, both compute 0+1=1 and write 1. Final result: 1. If one completes before the other starts reading, the second reads 1, writes 2. Final result: 2. The increment is not atomic — it involves a read, an add, and a write — so interleaving can produce either result.

questions.question: A server handles requests that are 90% waiting on database I/O and 10% CPU computation. The machine has 4 CPU cores. What is a reasonable thread pool size?
options: 4 threads (one per core)
Around 40 threads (cores / CPU fraction = 4 / 0.1)
1,000 threads for maximum parallelism
1 thread using an event loop only
questions.explanation: For I/O-bound work, the optimal thread count is approximately cores / (1 - I/O fraction) = 4 / 0.1 = 40. Since threads spend 90% of their time waiting on I/O, you can keep 40 threads active and still only saturate 4 cores during their 10% CPU bursts. Too few threads wastes CPU; too many wastes memory.

questions.question: Four conditions must ALL be present for deadlock to occur (Coffman conditions). Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is non-sharable
Starvation: a thread is perpetually denied access to a resource
Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another
Circular wait: a cycle exists in the resource-dependency graph
questions.explanation: The four Coffman conditions for deadlock are: (1) Mutual exclusion, (2) Hold and wait, (3) No preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and (4) Circular wait. Starvation is a different problem — a thread being indefinitely delayed — but it does not cause deadlock.
